presentingComplaint: 6 days of fever, dry cough, and progressively worsening breathlessness, now breathless at rest
history: Previously well 58-year-old man, unvaccinated for COVID-19, presents with a 6-day history of fever, myalgia, and dry cough. Over the last 48 hours he has developed progressive exertional dyspnoea now present at rest, with subjective chest tightness but no true pleuritic pain. No purulent sputum. No recent travel or sick contacts identified beyond a household member with confirmed COVID-19 10 days ago. No significant past medical history; non-smoker. No diarrhoea, no rash, no urinary symptoms.
examination: Alert, mildly tachypnoeic, speaking in short sentences, using accessory muscles of respiration. Bilateral fine end-inspiratory crepitations, most pronounced at the lung bases, no wheeze, no dullness to suggest consolidation or effusion. No cyanosis at rest on room air but desaturates on exertion. No lower limb oedema, no rash, no lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular exam unremarkable, abdomen soft and non-tender.
imaging: CT chest: bilateral, peripheral and basal-predominant ground-glass opacities with a crazy-paving pattern; no lobar consolidation, no pleural effusion
CXR: bilateral peripheral hazy infiltrates, worse at bases, no focal consolidation
microbiology: Blood cultures x2: no growth at 48h
Sputum Gram stain/culture: normal flora, no organism isolated
Urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella antigen: negative
differentialDiagnoses: Other viral pneumonia (influenza, other respiratory viruses)
Acute interstitial lung disease / organizing pneumonia
finalDiagnosis: COVID-19 pneumonia with hypoxaemic respiratory failure (bilateral ground-glass opacities)
stewardship: Not a primary bacterial infection; empirical antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless secondary bacterial pneumonia is suspected (e.g., purulent sputum, lobar consolidation, elevated procalcitonin, or clinical deterioration suggesting superinfection). Low procalcitonin and absence of consolidation here argue against empirical antibacterial therapy; if started pending cultures, de-escalate/stop by 48-72h if bacterial workup remains negative. Management is supportive: supplemental oxygen titrated to target SpO2, systemic corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) for patients requiring supplemental oxygen, consideration of antiviral therapy (e.g., remdesivir) per eligibility, and monitoring for thromboprophylaxis and clinical deterioration.
contraindications: Avoid empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics without evidence of bacterial co-infection
Corticosteroids should not be started before oxygen requirement is confirmed (harm signal in patients not requiring oxygen per RECOVERY trial)
Avoid remdesivir in significant renal impairment per product labelling (check eGFR)
